summary: Verified evidence supports a calibrated message, not 'a red light makes pedestrians ill'. Randomised crossover walks on a busy London street (diesel-dominated, 2 h) caused small, mostly symptom-free lung-function dips of up to 6.1% in adults with asthma (McCreanor 2007) and blunted walking benefits in older adults, with more symptoms in COPD (Sinharay 2018). In Taipei, personal PM2.5 was highest on scooter trips (53.6 ug/m3 vs 21.7 on the subway) with small PM2.5-associated rises in blood pressure, heart rate and an oxidative-stress marker in scooter and walking modes (Chuang 2020; healthy adults, riders not bystanders). Taiwanese panels link minutes-to-hours particle exposure to lower heart rate variability (Chuang 2005; Lung 2025). Daily ambient PM2.5/NO2 is linked to children's pneumonia visits and COPD admissions in Taiwanese cities, from city monitors, not roadsides. Time in traffic raised odds of MI within an hour in Germany (Peters 2004), mostly car travel. Milan data show transport is the most intense per minute yet a minority of daily dose. No study measures pedestrians at scooter-filled red lights or shows a single light causes disease. CO, chamber, UFP, odour and WHO text remain unverified.

findings.claim: In 60 adults with mild or moderate asthma, a 2-hour walk along a busy London street caused small, symptom-free but consistent drops in lung function compared with a walk in a park, with inflammatory markers rising.
findings.value: FEV1 down by up to 6.1%, FVC down by up to 5.4% (P=0.04 and P=0.01 for overall effect of exposure vs Hyde Park); sputum myeloperoxidase 24.5 vs 4.24 ng/mL (P=0.05); maximum airway pH decrease 1.9% vs 0.04% (P=0.003); effects greater in moderate than mild asthma; associated most consistently with ultrafine particles and elemental carbon
findings.setting: London (Oxford Street vs Hyde Park), 2 h walk, randomised crossover, 60 adults with mild or moderate asthma; diesel traffic
findings.citation: McCreanor J, Cullinan P, Nieuwenhuijsen MJ, Stewart-Evans J, et al. 2007. Respiratory effects of exposure to diesel traffic in persons with asthma. N Engl J Med 357(23):2348-2358.
findings.design: Randomised crossover; each participant walked 2 h along Oxford Street and, on a separate occasion, through Hyde Park, with real-time exposure, physiological and immunological measurements.
findings.quote: Walking for 2 hours on Oxford Street induced asymptomatic but consistent reductions in the forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) (up to 6.1%) and forced vital capacity (FVC) (up to 5.4%)
findings.caveats: Diesel traffic (the paper's own title), not scooters. 2 h of continuous walking, not seconds-to-minutes at a light. Adults with asthma only. Effects were asymptomatic. Associated most consistently with ultrafine particles and elemental carbon. Author list truncated to the four verified via Crossref.
findings.useOnSite: A two-hour walk along a heavily trafficked London street produced measurable, symptom-free dips in lung function in adults with asthma compared with a park walk (diesel-dominated traffic).
findings.verifierNote: Numbers and quote confirmed in the abstract (Europe PMC, Crossref: 357(23):2348-2358, 2007). The researcher's PubMed URL 18032763 is WRONG: that PMID is a lenalidomide myeloma paper. Correct PMID is 18057337. Added P-values and the moderate>mild finding.

findings.claim: In adults aged 60+ (healthy, stable COPD, stable ischaemic heart disease), a 2-hour walk on Oxford Street, compared with Hyde Park, attenuated the beneficial lung-function and arterial-stiffness responses to walking, and COPD patients reported more respiratory symptoms.
findings.value: COPD after Oxford St vs Hyde Park: sputum OR 3.15 (1.39-7.13), wheeze OR 4.00 (1.52-10.50), cough OR 1.95 (0.96-3.95, p<0.1), shortness of breath OR 1.86 (0.97-3.57, p<0.1); beneficial FEV1/FVC rise and PWV/augmentation-index fall seen in Hyde Park were attenuated on Oxford St up to 26 h after the walk
findings.setting: London, 119 participants (40 healthy, 40 COPD GOLD stage 2, 39 stable IHD), Oct 2012-Jun 2014, randomised crossover 2 h walks
findings.citation: Sinharay R, Gong J, Barratt B, Ohman-Strickland P, et al. 2018. Respiratory and cardiovascular responses to walking down a traffic-polluted road compared with walking in a traffic-free area in participants aged 60 years and older with chronic lung or heart disease and age-matched healthy controls: a randomised, crossover study. Lancet 391(10118):339-349.
findings.design: Randomised crossover, 2 h walk on Oxford Street vs Hyde Park; black carbon, PM, UFP and NO2 measured during walks; lung function and cardiovascular measures up to 26 h later.
findings.quote: Short-term exposure to traffic pollution prevents the beneficial cardiopulmonary effects of walking in people with COPD, ischaemic heart disease, and those free from chronic cardiopulmonary diseases.
findings.caveats: Urban London street, traffic pollution (not scooter-specific). 2 h exposure. Stable, clinically stable disease (COPD GOLD stage 2, i.e. moderate; stable IHD). The finding is attenuation of walking benefit, not an acute event. Several ORs only borderline (p<0.1). Authors note medication might reduce effects in IHD.
findings.useOnSite: For older adults, including those with COPD or heart disease, two hours on a busy traffic street blunted the benefits of walking and worsened respiratory symptoms in COPD compared with a park (London, not scooter-specific).
findings.verifierNote: All ORs, sample sizes, dates, quote confirmed in the abstract (Europe PMC, PMID 29221643, Lancet 391(10118):339-349). Minor wording fix: COPD was GOLD stage 2 (moderate), not 'mild-to-moderate'; symptom ORs apply to COPD only.

findings.claim: Time spent in traffic (car, public transport, motorcycle or bicycle) was associated with higher odds of myocardial infarction within the following hour.
findings.value: OR 2.92 (95% CI 2.22-3.83) for MI onset within 1 h after traffic exposure; OR 2.73 (2.06-3.61) after adjusting for exercise on a bicycle or getting up in the morning
findings.setting: Augsburg, Germany; 691 MI survivors, Feb 1999-Jul 2001; case-crossover from patient diaries
findings.citation: Peters A, von Klot S, Heier M, et al. 2004. Exposure to traffic and the onset of myocardial infarction. N Engl J Med 351(17):1721-1730.
findings.design: Case-crossover using the Augsburg (KORA) MI registry and 4-day activity diaries.
findings.quote: An association was found between exposure to traffic and the onset of a myocardial infarction within one hour afterward (odds ratio, 2.92; 95 percent confidence interval, 2.22 to 3.83; P<0.001).
findings.caveats: Exposure means time spent travelling (car most common source), not standing beside a road; includes stress, noise and exertion, so pollution is not isolated. Self-reported diary data. Motorcycle and bicycle pooled. Absolute risk per trip is very small. The authors conclude traffic 'may increase the risk ... in susceptible persons'.
findings.useOnSite: A German study found that people who had a heart attack were more likely to have been in traffic in the previous hour; this shows an association, not that standing at a red light causes a heart attack.
findings.verifierNote: Abstract confirmed via Europe PMC (PMID 15496621; 351(17):1721-1730). Crossref lookup for this DOI failed; citation data from PubMed/Europe PMC. Only the first three authors are shown, as in the researcher draft; the full list was not independently checked.

findings.claim: In 120 healthy Taipei adults, personal PM2.5 was highest while commuting by scooter, and PM2.5 was associated with higher systolic blood pressure, heart rate and urinary 8-OHdG (oxidative DNA damage marker) in the walking and scooter modes.
findings.value: PM2.5 scooter 53.6 +/- 26.1 vs subway 21.7 +/- 5.8 ug/m3; PM2.5-associated SBP +6.5% (walking), +7.9% (scooter); HR +3.4% (walking), +6.4% (scooter); 8-OHdG +8.1% (walking), +8.9% (scooter); not significant in subway mode or when walking with a facemask (BP and HR)
findings.setting: Taipei, Taiwan; 120 healthy adults; six commuting modes (subway, gasoline bus, gasoline car, gasoline scooter, walking, walking with facemask); measurements 09:00-10:00
findings.citation: Chuang K-J, Lin L-Y, Ho K-F, Su C-T. 2020. Traffic-related PM2.5 exposure and its cardiovascular effects among healthy commuters in Taipei, Taiwan. Atmospheric Environment: X 7:100084.
findings.design: Repeated-measures panel; six repeated measurements per participant (one per commuting mode); mixed-effects models of PM2.5 against SBP, DBP, HR and urinary 8-OHdG.
findings.quote: The PM2.5 level (Mean ± SD) was the highest in the scooter mode (53.6 ± 26.1 μg/m3) but the lowest in the subway mode (21.7 ± 5.8 μg/m3).
findings.caveats: Healthy adults, one morning hour per mode. The scooter mode is the rider's own exposure, not a pedestrian standing beside idling scooters. The abstract does not give the PM2.5 increment to which the % changes refer, so quote them only as direction and rough size. Small physiological shifts, not disease. Abstract read via OpenAlex; full text not opened.
findings.useOnSite: A Taipei panel of 120 healthy adults found the highest personal PM2.5 on scooter trips and small PM2.5-associated rises in blood pressure, heart rate and an oxidative-stress marker in scooter and walking modes.
findings.verifierNote: Crossref metadata (Atmos Environ X 7:100084, 2020; Chuang, Lin, Ho, Su) and full abstract via OpenAlex confirm every number. Not indexed in Europe PMC.

findings.claim: In Taipei cardiac and hypertensive patients, submicron particles (0.3-1.0 um) at 1-4 h moving averages were associated with reduced heart rate variability; larger fractions were not.
findings.value: Per interquartile increase in PM0.3-1.0: SDNN down 1.49-4.88%, r-MSSD down 2.73-8.25%; no association with PM1.0-2.5 or PM2.5-10
findings.setting: Taipei, Taiwan; 10 coronary heart disease and 16 pre-/hypertensive patients; ambulatory ECG with personal PM measurements
findings.citation: Chuang K-J, Chan C-C, Chen N-T, Su T-C, Lin L-Y. 2005. Effects of particle size fractions on reducing heart rate variability in cardiac and hypertensive patients. Environ Health Perspect 113(12):1693-1697.
findings.design: Panel study; linear mixed-effects models of log10 HRV indices on 1-4 h moving-average PM exposures, adjusted for personal and environmental attributes.
findings.quote: For an interquartile increase in PM(0.3-1.0), there were 1.49-4.88% decreases in SDNN and 2.73-8.25% decreases in r-MSSD.
findings.caveats: Only 26 patients; exposure is general personal exposure, not traffic-specific; HRV is a surrogate marker; interquartile range not stated in the abstract.
findings.useOnSite: A small Taipei panel of cardiac and hypertensive patients showed lower heart rate variability within hours of higher submicron particle exposure.
findings.verifierNote: Crossref and Europe PMC confirm 113(12):1693-1697, 2005, authors, and all numbers. Volume now verified.

findings.claim: In seven healthy older Taipei residents followed for 72 h, personal exposure to particles, black carbon, PAHs and CO was associated with changes in heart rate and heart-rate-variability indices, with delayed effects after 1-8 h.
findings.value: n/a in abstract (direction of effects only; effects mixed across pollutants and indices)
findings.setting: Taipei metropolitan area, 7 healthy older adults, 72 h personal monitoring with portable ECG, GAMM
findings.citation: Tang CS, Chuang KJ, Chang TY, Chuang HC, Chen LH, Lung SC, Chang LT. 2019. Effects of Personal Exposures to Micro- and Nano-Particulate Matter, Black Carbon, Particle-Bound Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons, and Carbon Monoxide on Heart Rate Variability in a Panel of Healthy Older Subjects. Int J Environ Res Public Health 16(23):4672.
findings.design: Personal exposure monitoring plus ECG; generalised additive mixed models.
findings.quote: Since the small sample size would limit the generalizability of this study, more studies with larger scale are warranted
findings.caveats: n=7; mixed directions (several HRV indices rose with some pollutants, CO lowered others); not traffic-specific; unsuitable for effect sizes. Original quote in the findings was a paraphrase; the abstract wording is given here.
findings.useOnSite: Do not cite as a headline; at most mention that small Taiwanese panels link personal exposure to heart-rate changes, with the authors cautioning about sample size.
findings.verifierNote: Crossref and Europe PMC abstract confirm n=7, design, delayed effects and the small-sample caveat. Quote corrected to actual abstract wording.

findings.claim: In Kaohsiung children, short-term rises in PM2.5 and NO2 were associated with more emergency-department visits for pneumonia.
findings.value: Per IQR increment 3 days before the event, odds of an ED pneumonia visit up 14.0% for PM2.5 (95% CI 5.1-23.8%), 14.1% for NO2 (5.0-24.1%), 10.9% for PM10, 4.5% for SO2; older children (>=4 y) more susceptible to PM2.5
findings.setting: Kaohsiung City, Taiwan, 2008-2014, 4,024 ED visits for pneumonia in patients aged <=17 y, 11 monitoring stations
findings.citation: Cheng CY, Cheng SY, Chen CC, Pan HY, Wu KH, Cheng FJ. 2019. Ambient air pollution is associated with pediatric pneumonia: a time-stratified case-crossover study in an urban area. Environ Health 18:77.
findings.design: Time-stratified case-crossover; single- and two-pollutant models.
findings.quote: Short-term exposure to PM2.5 and NO2 possibly plays an important role in pediatric pneumonia in Kaohsiung, Taiwan.
findings.caveats: Ambient city-wide monitor concentrations (daily), not roadside or scooter-specific; association at a 3-day lag, not minutes; NO2 is a traffic marker but has many sources.
findings.useOnSite: In Kaohsiung, days with higher PM2.5 and NO2 were followed by more children's ED visits for pneumonia.
findings.verifierNote: PubMed full abstract (PMID 31462279) confirms all numbers and the conclusion sentence.

findings.claim: Taiwanese NHI data show asthma ER visits are associated with outdoor air pollution and weather, with children (particularly young girls) more susceptible than adults.
findings.value: Abstract gives only: 1 C temperature rise protective, OR 0.981 (0.971-0.991) children and 0.985 (0.975-0.994) adults; no pollutant-specific ORs in abstract
findings.setting: Taiwan, NHI Research Database asthma ER visits, EPA monitoring data (SO2, NO2, O3, CO, PM2.5, PM10), bi-directional case-crossover
findings.citation: Yu HR, Lin CR, Tsai JH, Hsieh YT, Tsai TA, Tsai CK, Lee YC, Liu TY, Tsai CM, Chen CC, Chang CH, Hsu TY, Niu CK. 2020. A Multifactorial Evaluation of the Effects of Air Pollution and Meteorological Factors on Asthma Exacerbation. Int J Environ Res Public Health 17(11):4010.
findings.design: Bi-directional case-crossover of NHIRD asthma ER visits against monitor pollution and meteorology.
findings.quote: Children, especially younger females, are more susceptible to asthma AE due to the effects of outdoor air pollution than adults.
findings.caveats: Ambient monitor data; abstract gives no pollutant ORs; the authors emphasise meteorology as a major modulator. Not traffic- or scooter-specific.
findings.useOnSite: Taiwanese insurance data suggest children are more susceptible than adults to asthma flare-ups linked to outdoor air pollution.
findings.verifierNote: PubMed abstract (PMID 32512940) confirms quote and temperature ORs; authors list completed from PubMed.

findings.claim: In Taipei, higher daily PM2.5 was associated with more COPD hospital admissions, more strongly on warm days.
findings.value: Per IQR rise in PM2.5 (single-pollutant model): +12% (95% CI 8-16%) on warm days (>23 C), +3% (0-7%) on cool days; remained significant in two-pollutant models with SO2 or O3
findings.setting: Taipei, Taiwan, 2006-2010, case-crossover of COPD inpatient admissions
findings.citation: Tsai S-S, Chang C-C, Yang C-Y. 2013. Fine Particulate Air Pollution and Hospital Admissions for Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease: A Case-Crossover Study in Taipei. Int J Environ Res Public Health 10(11):6015-6026.
findings.design: Case-crossover controlling for weather, day of week, seasonality and trend; single- and two-pollutant models.
findings.quote: COPD admissions were significantly and positively associated with higher PM2.5 levels during both warm days (>23 °C) and cool days (<23 °C), with an interquartile range increase of 12% (95% CI = 8-16%) and 3% (95% CI = 0-7%) in COPD admissions, respectively.
findings.caveats: Daily ambient PM2.5 from city monitors; admissions, not ED visits; not scooter-specific; the 3% cool-day interval touches zero.
findings.useOnSite: In Taipei, higher daily PM2.5 was followed by more COPD hospital admissions.
findings.verifierNote: Numbers, quote and pages 6015-6026 confirmed. The researcher's PubMed URL 24217180 is WRONG (that PMID is a dioxin breast-milk paper); correct PMID is 24284359.

findings.claim: In a Taiwanese cohort, exposure to higher truck traffic volume was associated with higher cardiovascular mortality; small-car traffic showed a similar but non-significant direction; PM2.5 mediated over 60% of the traffic-CVD association.
findings.value: HR 1.24 (95% CI 1.03-1.51, P=0.03) per log-unit of truck volume; HR 1.10 (0.94-1.27, P=0.23, not significant) per log-unit of small-car volume; PM2.5 mediation >60%
findings.setting: Taiwan, 12,098 REVEAL-HBV participants, 382 CVD deaths 2000-2014; traffic counts from the Directorate General of Highway; LUR PM2.5
findings.citation: Pan WC, Yeh SY, Wu CD, Huang et al. 2021. Association Between Traffic Count and Cardiovascular Mortality: A Prospective Cohort Study in Taiwan. J Epidemiol 31(5):343-349.
findings.design: Prospective cohort with road traffic counts and LUR PM2.5; Cox models; causal mediation. Only the first four authors (Pan, Yeh, Wu, Huang) were verified via Crossref; use et al.
findings.quote: Exposure to exhaust from trucks or gasoline-powered cars is positively associated with CVD mortality, and air pollution may play a role in this association.
findings.caveats: Long-term exposure, not red-light minutes; scooters not analysed; the small-car result is not statistically significant, so the authors' conclusion is stronger than their own small-car number; cohort of HBV-screened adults.
findings.useOnSite: Long-term residence near heavy truck traffic is linked to higher cardiovascular mortality in Taiwan; this concerns years of exposure, not a single wait.
findings.verifierNote: Numbers confirmed. Issue is 31(5), not 31(6) (Crossref and PubMed). Claim reworded: significant association is for trucks only; small cars n.s. Cite as Pan WC, Yeh SY, Wu CD, et al.

findings.claim: In Milan children, most of the daily black carbon dose accrued at school and home (82%), but dose per unit time was highest during transport and outdoors, with the highest exposure peaks during the home-to-school commute.
findings.value: 82% of daily dose at school and home; mean EBC 1.3 +/- 1.5 (warm) and 3.9 +/- 3.3 (cold) ug/m3
findings.setting: Milan, Italy; 73 and 89 schoolchildren in two seasons; GPS and diaries; non-Taiwanese, car-dominated
findings.citation: Boniardi L, Dons E, Longhi F, Scuffi C, et al. 2021. Personal exposure to equivalent black carbon in children in Milan, Italy: Time-activity patterns and predictors by season. Environ Pollut 274:116530.
findings.design: Personal EBC monitoring with GPS, time-activity diaries and questionnaire; mixed-effect models.
findings.quote: Children received most of their daily dose at school and home (82%), but the highest dose/time intensity was related to transportation and outdoor environments.
findings.caveats: Transport share of daily dose is not stated in the abstract (only that 82% was at school and home, so at most 18% elsewhere including transport). Black carbon only. Italy, car-dominated. Author list truncated to the four verified via Crossref.
findings.useOnSite: Studies of children's daily dose show brief periods in transport are the most intense per minute but a minority of the daily total.
findings.verifierNote: Abstract and Crossref (Environ Pollut 274:116530, 2021; Boniardi, Dons, Longhi, Scuffi...) confirm all numbers. Use et al. in citation.

findings.claim: Motorised travel gave about 2.2 ug/m3 higher breathing-zone black carbon than walking, yet inhaled dose per 30 min was lower for motorised than walking trips because of lower ventilation.
findings.value: Breathing-zone BC vs walking: +2.20 (1.99-2.41) ug/m3 public transport, +2.29 (2.10-2.48) private motorised; inhaled BC dose per 30 min vs walking: -0.25 ug (-0.35 to -0.15) public transport, -0.19 ug (-0.28 to -0.10) private motorised
findings.setting: Grand Paris, 283 participants, 7,495 trip stages; personal MicroAeth monitors at the neck
findings.citation: Bista S, Dureau C, Chaix B, et al. 2022. Personal exposure to concentrations and inhalation of black carbon according to transport mode use: The MobiliSense sensor-based study. Environ Int 158:106990.
findings.design: Sensor-based trip-stage analysis with inhaled dose derived from accelerometry, heart-rate and breathing-rate ventilation estimates; mixed models.
findings.quote: Trip stages involving public transport and private motorized transport were associated with a 2.20 µg/m3 (95% CI: 1.99, 2.41) and 2.29 µg/m3 (95% CI: 2.10, 2.48) higher breathing zone concentration to BC than walking, respectively.
findings.caveats: Shows concentration is not dose; active travellers breathe more per minute. Standing still at a kerb is not covered (dose would then be lower than when walking). Paris, not Taiwan; mode-level comparison, not red-light measurement. Online Dec 2021, issue year 2022.
findings.useOnSite: Concentration alone does not equal dose; ventilation rate matters, so a pedestrian breathing hard beside traffic may inhale substantial doses.
findings.verifierNote: Numbers confirmed in abstract. The quoted line 'had a 0.41 ug higher inhaled dose' in the draft refers to OTHER ACTIVE modes (e.g. cycling), not to motorised vs walking; replaced with the correct sentence. Year is 2022 (vol 158) per Crossref/PubMed.

findings.claim: WHO 2021 Global Air Quality Guidelines set CO at 4 mg/m3 (24 h); older 8 h (10), 1 h (35) and 15 min (100 mg/m3) values are reported as retained; for ultrafine particles WHO gave good-practice statements rather than a guideline value.
findings.value: CO 4 mg/m3 24 h; 10 mg/m3 8 h; 35 mg/m3 1 h; 100 mg/m3 15 min; no UFP numerical guideline
findings.citation: World Health Organization. 2021. WHO global air quality guidelines: particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10), ozone, nitrogen dioxide, sulfur dioxide and carbon monoxide. Geneva: WHO. ISBN 9789240034228.
findings.design: Guideline document. Not opened: the NCBI Bookshelf page returned a bot-challenge page to this verifier, and WHO hosts were not reachable.
findings.caveats: Neither the researcher nor this verifier opened the WHO text; the quoted sentence came from an IQAir summary. The 15 min/1 h/8 h values are historically from WHO indoor guidelines. Must be checked against the WHO PDF before publication. No peer-reviewed secondary source was found in Europe PMC that states the UFP wording (search returned only the WHO systematic-review introduction, Environ Int 2022, 10.1016/j.envint.2022.107556, not checked for UFP content).
findings.useOnSite: Do not publish WHO CO or UFP wording until it has been checked against the WHO report text.
findings.verifierNote: Could not open any source that settles it. Confidence downgraded from SECONDARY to UNVERIFIED because the only support was a commercial summary. The quote field is blank rather than carry an unverified quotation.

findings.claim: Taiwanese (Kaohsiung) and Indonesian (Bandung) panels wearing microsensors showed short 5-minute PM2.5 peaks and immediate small decreases in heart rate variability with 5-minute PM2.5 and PM1; in Indonesia the effect was shown in scooter subjects.
findings.value: Kaohsiung (55 subjects, 2019-2020): mean 5-min PM2.5 14.9 +/- 11.2 ug/m3, maximum 5-min peak PM2.5 467.4 ug/m3; HRV change -0.9% to -2.5% per 10 ug/m3 increase in PM2.5 or PM1 (larger for PM1); main identified sources were community factories, mosquito-coil, agricultural waste and incense burning
findings.setting: Bandung, Indonesia (50 subjects, 2018-2019) and Kaohsiung, Taiwan (55 subjects, 2019-2020); AS-LUNG PM sensors and RootiRx HRV sensors; generalized additive mixed models
findings.citation: Lung SC, Tsou MM, Cheng CC, Setyawati W. 2025. Peaks, sources, and immediate health impacts of PM2.5 and PM1 exposure in Indonesia and Taiwan with microsensors. J Expo Sci Environ Epidemiol 35(2):264-277.
findings.design: Panel with personal microsensors and activity records; GAMM of 5-min exposures against HRV indices and heart rate.
findings.quote: The HRV change for a 10 µg/m3 increase in PM2.5 and PM1 ranged from -0.9% to -2.5% except for ratio of low-high frequency
findings.caveats: Added by verifier. Closest verified Taiwanese evidence that minutes-scale PM peaks track immediate HRV changes, but the identified Taiwan sources were not traffic; traffic or scooter exhaust is not quantified in the abstract. Panel of about 55 people, not a general-population risk. HRV is a surrogate marker.
findings.useOnSite: A Taiwanese panel using wearable sensors found that 5-minute PM2.5 peaks were followed by small immediate drops in heart rate variability (about 1-2.5% per 10 ug/m3), though the main peak sources identified there were not traffic.
findings.verifierNote: Found by Europe PMC search; abstract read in PubMed (PMID 38806636). Fills part of the gap on minutes-scale Taiwanese effects.

findings.claim: Taiwanese food-delivery workers, who spend their working day in traffic, had higher exhaled-air carbon monoxide than a reference group, even after separating smokers.
findings.value: Exhaled CO 4.79 ppm (156 workers) vs 1.51 ppm (49 reference), p<0.001; non-smokers 1.57 vs 1.13 ppm (p=0.002); smokers 14.46 vs 1.57 ppm; smoking may account for ~89% of CO in exhaled air among smokers
findings.setting: Taiwan (NCKU group), 156 online food-delivery workers vs 49 reference; breath CO plus questionnaire
findings.citation: Li KH, Cheng YY, Huang SC, Chen CA, Lu JY, Chao ZT, Tseng YC, Guo HR. 2025. Assessing Carbon Monoxide Exposure in Food Delivery Workers by Using Exhaled Air with Consideration of Smoking Habits. J Epidemiol Glob Health 15(1):124.
findings.design: Cross-sectional comparison of exhaled CO between workers and a reference group.
findings.quote: amongst non-smokers, the CO concentration was still higher in food delivery workers than in the reference group (1.57 ppm vs. 1.13 ppm, p = 0.002)
findings.caveats: Added by verifier. Occupational, full-shift, mostly riders (the abstract does not say scooter), not pedestrians at a light. Exhaled CO in ppm is not carboxyhaemoglobin and is not comparable with WHO ambient mg/m3 values. The non-smoker difference is about 0.4 ppm. Smoking dominates.
findings.useOnSite: Do not use as evidence of red-light CO exposure. At most: a 2025 Taiwanese study found slightly higher breath CO in non-smoking food-delivery workers than in a reference group.
findings.verifierNote: Found via Europe PMC; abstract read in PubMed (PMID 41114904). Only Taiwanese CO exposure study located; it does not address roadside CO against WHO guidelines.

doNotClaim: That standing at one red light causes asthma, heart disease, cancer or any chronic disease; no study demonstrates this.
That the London walking studies (McCreanor 2007; Sinharay 2018) show effects of scooter exhaust; they are diesel-dominated urban traffic and 2 h walks.
That Peters 2004 shows that traffic exposure (time in vehicles, mostly cars, with stress, noise and exertion) is equivalent to standing near idling scooters.
That scooters are more harmful per vehicle than cars or diesel buses; none of the verified studies compare emission toxicity per vehicle.
That the Taipei commuter study (Chuang 2020) measured pedestrians waiting beside idling scooters; its scooter mode is the rider's own exposure over one morning hour.
That Taiwanese ED/hospital time-series studies (city-wide daily PM2.5/NO2) measure roadside red-light exposure or attribute events to scooters.
Any specific WHO CO or UFP wording; the WHO report text was not opened by researcher or verifier.
That the bad smell of exhaust is a measured health outcome or a proxy for a specific concentration; no study located quantifies odour against dose.

That gas-phase CO at a red light reaches carboxyhaemoglobin levels of concern; no roadside CO or carboxyhaemoglobin evidence was verified. The 2025 breath-CO study (Li) is occupational and not comparable with WHO ambient values.
Effect sizes (% changes) from single small panels (n=7, n=26, n=55, n=120) as general-population risks.
That Pan 2021 shows small-car or scooter traffic raises CVD mortality; only the truck HR was statistically significant.
That Lung 2025 identifies traffic as the source of the Taiwanese PM peaks; the sources named were factories, mosquito coils, agricultural and incense burning.
The PubMed links given in the researcher draft for McCreanor (18032763) and Tsai (24217180); they point to unrelated papers.
gaps: Taiwan roadside or intersection CO concentrations versus WHO 15-min/1-h/8-h values: not found in searches by researcher or verifier.
Carboxyhaemoglobin and symptoms at roadside CO concentrations: no verified source.
Controlled chamber studies of gasoline exhaust (and that most chamber studies use diesel): not searched to a verified source.

Measured ultrafine particle or black carbon peaks at scooter-dense red lights, stop lines or two-stage left-turn boxes (Taiwan, Hanoi, HCMC, Bangkok, Jakarta): not found; two Europe PMC searches returned nothing relevant.

Studies quantifying the share of daily exposure from short periods in traffic in Taiwan or Asia: only Boniardi 2021 (Milan) verified; Dons et al. Flanders BC time-activity work was not located in a verifiable form (Europe PMC search returned only Boniardi, Dons co-author, and unrelated BC papers).
